title: The Spire of the Weeping Wood
premise: Tamsin Vane, a hedge-witch hiding as a charm-seller in the magic-outlawed city of Corvane, inherits a dying stranger's map to the Spire of the Weeping Wood—a living door out of a country that was magically erased from the world's memory twelve years ago. Hunted by the Pale Office and shadowed by the stranger's vengeful daughter, Tamsin learns they are the last living anchor of the erased nation's gate, and that opening the door will restore the country but demand a memory in payment. In the Spire, Tamsin must choose between surrendering their own past to resurrect a nation's, and in the end they give up their name and history to open the door, becoming the Spire's new keeper while the freed country blooms beyond it.
about_author: Freya Kavanagh is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the letters of displaced communities before turning to fiction. She writes from a crooked house on a northern coast, where she keeps an unreasonable number of keys that open nothing.

chapters.title: Charms for the Forgetful
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In Corvane, Tamsin sells harmless charms—luck knots, sleep salts—while concealing their true gift. A routine day establishes their careful invisibility and the city's quiet fear of magic. The emotional beat is weary vigilance: Tamsin has made safety a craft, and believes they have perfected it.

chapters.title: The Stranger at the Threshold
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A bleeding stranger staggers into the shop at closing, presses a folded map into Tamsin's hands, and dies whispering the name 'Vesperholt'—a country Tamsin has never heard of, yet the map is drawn in their own handwriting. The beat is dread: the stranger's death marks Tamsin's door, literally, with the Pale Office's chalk sigil.

chapters.title: Chalk and Ash
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Office inquisitor Merrick Hale arrives to 'question' Tamsin, revealing the stranger was an escaped anchor-keeper. Tamsin lies badly, burns the map's copy, and discovers the original cannot burn. The beat is fear curdling into resolve: staying means the gallows, so flight becomes the only honest option.

chapters.title: The Daughter of Vesperholt
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Tamsin flees the city and is ambushed by Sera Ilves, the dead stranger's daughter, who blames Tamsin for her father's death. Forced into uneasy alliance, Sera explains the Weeping Wood and the erased country. The beat is friction and grudging recognition: two people guarding the same wound from opposite sides.

chapters.title: What the River Remembers
chapters.summary: Sera's POV. The pair follows the map down a river that runs backward at dusk, through villages where no one can say what lies east. Tamsin's suppressed memories begin leaking—songs they shouldn't know, a lullaby in a dead tongue. The beat is uncanny grief: identity is not what Tamsin thought, and the map's handwriting was no accident.

chapters.title: The Pale Office Closes
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. The inquisitor, himself a conscript of the Office, tracks the pair and reveals the Office's secret: the erasure of Vesperholt was the Office's founding crime, sustained by feeding memories to the Spire. The beat is moral vertigo—hunter and hunted are both prisoners of the same lie, and Hale begins to doubt.

chapters.title: The Weeping Wood
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They reach the forest where trees bleed sap like tears and each trunk holds a stolen memory. Touching one, Tamsin recovers the night of the erasure: they were a child anchor, smuggled out, their past deliberately cut away. The beat is devastating recognition—the price of survival was Tamsin's whole self.

chapters.title: The Gate That Should Stay Shut
chapters.summary: Sera's POV. At the Spire's door, the Office's forces arrive; Hale, ordered to burn the Wood, instead turns on his superiors and is struck down buying the pair time. Sera learns opening the gate requires an anchor's complete memory—her father died refusing to pay it. The beat is sacrifice and rage: love demands a cost no one wants to name.

chapters.title: The Price of the Door
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax. Inside the Spire, Tamsin confronts the gate and the residue of the erased nation—millions of memories screaming to be whole. Tamsin chooses to pay: name, history, self, surrendered so a country can exist again. The beat is terrible, luminous choice; Sera holds the door's edge and speaks Tamsin's name one last time so something of them remains.

chapters.title: A Country, Remembered
chapters.summary: Sera's POV, resolution. Vesperholt floods back into the world; maps redraw themselves and the grieving villages remember what lies east. Tamsin, now nameless and new, remains as the Spire's keeper—unremembered by all but Sera, who visits with the lullaby. The beat is bittersweet renewal: identity can be given away, but not erased, when someone carries it for you.
